title: The size and structure of the adult social care sector and workforce in England, 2026
key_claim: England's adult social care vacancy rate fell to 6.2% in 2025/26, the lowest since 2015/16, equivalent to roughly 96,000 vacancies, down 10.5% on the previous year; filled posts rose 1.4% to 1.59 million (22,000 more, a fourth consecutive year of growth but the slowest in four years); posts filled by British-nationality workers fell by 40,000 over the year and by 130,000 since 2020/21; new international workers joining directly from abroad fell to 30,000 in 2025/26, the lowest in four years, down from 50,000 in 2024/25 and 105,000 in 2023/24; the sector will need an additional 410,000 posts by 2040.
frame_summary: The definitive workforce dataset presents a record-low vacancy rate and a growing workforce while documenting that both the international and domestic recruitment streams feeding that workforce are shrinking simultaneously.
notes: Tier 1 primary workforce dataset (ASC-WDS, 750,000+ records across 21,000+ locations). Anchor for the headline-vs-pipeline tension.

title: Immigration system statistics, year ending March 2026: summary of latest statistics
key_claim: There were 253,000 work visas granted in the year ending March 2026, 17% fewer than the previous year and 59% fewer than the YE December 2023 peak; 111,000 Skilled Worker visas were granted, 76% below the peak, a fall driven by Health and Care visas, with visas issued to main applicants in a Caring Personal Service occupation falling from 108,000 to 1,400; changes implemented on 22 July 2025 ended overseas recruitment for care workers.
frame_summary: Official immigration statistics show the Health and Care visa route that drove care-sector recruitment has been closed almost to zero, removing the mechanism that supplied the recent migrant care workforce.
notes: Tier 1 Accredited Official Statistics. Quantifies the closure of the overseas care pipeline.

title: Social care 360: workforce and carers
date_evidence: Social care 360: workforce and carers (Long read) - 8 Apr 2026
key_claim: Between 2023/24 and 2024/25 the adult social care vacancy rate fell from 8.3% to 7.0% (126,000 to 111,000 vacancies), driven by overseas recruitment: around 185,000 people started direct care roles after arriving from abroad between March 2022 and March 2024, plus a further 50,000 in 2024/25, while the number of UK domestic workers fell by 85,000 since 2020/21; the monthly tracker put the vacancy rate at 6.7% in November 2025; the government has legislated for a fair pay agreement backed by GBP 500 million, with the first agreement not expected before 2027, and in December 2025 proposed that Health and Care visa arrivals wait 15 years for permanent residence; an experienced care worker now earns just 7p an hour more than one on their first day.
frame_summary: The King's Fund attributes the entire fall in care vacancies to a one-off surge in overseas recruitment, while the domestic workforce shrinks and the policy meant to replace international supply will not take effect for years.
notes: Tier 2 institutional analysis. Establishes that the vacancy fall is migrant-driven and that the domestic pipeline is contracting.

title: Net migration: Frequently asked questions
date_evidence: Net migration: Frequently asked questions - 24 May 2026 (dateline below title)
key_claim: Net migration fell from a post-pandemic peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023 to 171,000 in 2025, largely due to 2024 visa restrictions including closer scrutiny of care-sector sponsorship following reports of widespread exploitation; the decline may prove temporary, because once migrants who arrived earlier in the decade leave, emigration will fall and net migration is expected to tick back up; care visas may help reduce the cost of providing care in the short run but do not address the sector's fundamental recruitment problem, namely poor pay and conditions.
frame_summary: The Migration Observatory argues the migration fall is real and partly justified by exploitation concerns, but warns it may be temporary and that visas never fixed the sector's underlying pay-and-conditions problem.
notes: Tier 2 counter-source: gives the strongest case that restriction is defensible and that the underlying problem is pay, not visas.

title: Adult social care vacancy rate falls to decade low but challenges persist
key_claim: Reporting the Skills for Care 2026 data, the vacancy rate fell to 6.2% (roughly 96,000 vacancies, around three times the wider economy), British-nationality posts fell by 40,000 over the year and 130,000 since 2020/21, new international workers from abroad fell to 30,000, and demand will rise by 410,000 posts by 2040; Skills for Care CEO Oonagh Smyth said domestic workforce numbers are falling and there is no dedicated visa route for international recruitment.
frame_summary: Trade coverage frames the decade-low vacancy rate as progress shadowed by a falling domestic workforce and the loss of the international recruitment route, quoting the sector body's own caution.
verbatim_quote: no dedicated visa route for international recruitment
notes: Tier 3 journalism corroborating Skills for Care figures. quote_provenance manually-verified: the page's 403 bot-block prevents the audit fetcher, but the WebFetch on 2026-06-28 returned CEO Oonagh Smyth verbatim: 'domestic workforce numbers are falling and there is no dedicated visa route for international recruitment - all of which highlight the scale of the challenge ahead.'

title: 'Progress on paper, precarity in practise': The Care Workers' Charity responds to falling vacancy rates
key_claim: The Care Workers' Charity warns that the falling vacancy rate is progress on paper but structural fragility in practice: around 235,000 overseas workers joined the sector since 2022 while the number of UK domestic workers fell by 85,000 since 2020/21, so the domestic pipeline is shrinking not recovering; the first fair pay agreement will not land until 2028 and its GBP 500 million is non-ringfenced, and the government has proposed a 15-year wait to settlement for Health and Care visa workers.
frame_summary: The charity argues the headline vacancy improvement masks a workforce that is simultaneously harder to recruit from abroad and failing to attract domestic staff, with the remedy arriving too late.
notes: Tier 3 trade/advocacy. Names the counter-counter directly: progress on paper, precarity in practice.

title: Skilled Worker visas in ninth consecutive decline, as fewer nurses, therapists and scientists come to the UK
key_claim: Visas granted for Caring Personal Service roles fell from 107,847 in 2023 to 3,178 in 2025 (just 23 in Q4 2025), despite Skills for Care data showing 78,330 roles vacant across adult social care in England as of January 2026 at a 6.3% vacancy rate; the decline extends across the health-and-care pipeline, with visas to Nursing Professionals down 93% (26,100 to 1,777) against 25,504 unfilled NHS registered-nursing vacancies in September 2025, and total Skilled Worker visas to main applicants at 45,797 in 2025, the lowest since the UK left the EU.
frame_summary: Work Rights Centre argues the government's migration cuts are working on their own terms but are severing the supply of care, nursing and other critical workers while domestic vacancies stay high.
notes: Tier 4 advocacy, used as the single structural anchor (3-6m band) for the cross-occupational scale of the visa decline. Treat directionally.
